extracted.intended_audience: aspiring single-panel cartoonists, especially those aiming for The New Yorker
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for producing single-panel cartoons suitable for The New Yorker, emphasizing idea generation, image-caption interplay, single-joke clarity, and developing a distinctive drawing style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect odd pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: collect odd PAIRS — two things that don't usually appear together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a running list of unexpected pairings; the incongruity between the two elements is the raw material for a cartoon idea. The emphasis is on pairing items that are not commonly associated to create surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore relationship between paired elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2: ask, what relationship would these two things have?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work out plausible or ironic relationships between the paired elements — power dynamics, misunderstandings, role reversals, or literal/metaphorical links that generate a concept for a scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define speakers and add voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 3: who would say what to whom in that relationship?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the characters, their voices, and what line (caption) would best reveal the humor inherent in their relationship. Thinking in terms of 'who says what to whom' helps produce a caption that completes the gag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write the caption last
rubrics_metrics.description: The caption is the LAST thing you write, not the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop the visual situation and specifics of the drawing first so the caption can act as the second beat that synthesizes meaning; avoid writing a caption that would stand alone without the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image-caption share meaning (image-caption lock)
rubrics_metrics.description: The image and caption must SHARE meaning, not duplicate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for interplay where the picture conveys something (X), the caption conveys something else (Y), and the audience mentally synthesizes a third meaning (Z). The image should add essential information; neither element should merely repeat the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption must not only describe the image
rubrics_metrics.description: A caption that just describes the image fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid captions that simply label what's visibly happening; the caption needs to add twist, context, or incongruity rather than restating the obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption must relate to the image
rubrics_metrics.description: A caption that has nothing to do with the image fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the caption connects to the scene and relies on visual cues; unrelated one-liners that ignore the drawing break the image-caption lock and weaken the cartoon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay/synthesis produces the joke
rubrics_metrics.description: The interplay (image says X, caption says Y, audience synthesizes Z) is the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design both visual and verbal beats so that the humor exists in their combination rather than in either element alone; think in two-beat structure where the audience must integrate both to get the gag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing must anchor a specific caption
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawing is too generic to anchor a specific caption (failure mode).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the art specific and concrete enough that it suggests a unique interpretive angle; generic backgrounds or indistinct characters make it hard to craft a caption that adds meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption must depend on the drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: The caption is a complete joke that doesn't need the drawing (failure mode).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the gag works as a standalone one-liner, the cartoon is likely misconstructed for the image-caption format — the caption should feel incomplete without the visual context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require two beats, not one
rubrics_metrics.description: The pair (image + caption) is one beat, not two — no synthesis required (failure mode).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid situations where image and caption simply state the same beat; successful cartoons require two complementary beats that together produce a third meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-joke rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A New Yorker cartoon has ONE joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus the cartoon on a single comic premise; multiple jokes or competing punchlines dilute impact and confuse the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid multiple competing jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple jokes confuse the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep background details or secondary elements neutral unless they directly support the single joke; avoid visual or verbal elements that create separate gags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutralize nonessential drawing elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawing's other elements should be neutral, not competing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use compositional restraint so only the elements necessary to the joke draw attention; extraneous detail can distract from the main beat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing style as comedic instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: A cartoonist's drawing style is a comedic instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a consistent style that performs comedic work — tonal range, rhythms, and visual assumptions of your style will shape the kinds of jokes that land. Style choices should support the humor rather than merely decorate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use style to add comedic register
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a style that does comedic work for you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how line quality, exaggeration, and visual metaphor contribute to tone; distinctive styles can suggest specific registers of humor and make otherwise familiar jokes feel fresh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original concept (Mankoff selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Original concept (not seen before).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors favor ideas that feel new or present familiar human truths in an unfamiliar way. Avoid rehashing widely circulated premises without a fresh twist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean execution (image-caption lock) (Mankoff selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clean execution (image and caption lock).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond the idea, the technical execution must align: the drawing and caption should interlock clearly and the joke should be readable at a glance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tonal fit for the magazine (Mankoff selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tonal fit for the magazine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider The New Yorker's sensibility — subtlety, irony, and a certain literate or observational tone — and whether the cartoon's voice matches that audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizability of human truth (Mankoff selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizability of human truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cartoons that make an observation about human behavior or social reality that readers instantly recognize tend to resonate. The humor should illuminate an identifiable truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dernavich working rubric — Is it one joke?
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. Is the cartoon ONE joke, not two?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a checklist question: if more than one comedic premise exists, simplify or remove competing beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dernavich working rubric — image/caption synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: 2. Do image and caption synthesize meaning, neither duplicating nor diverging?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm the image provides something the caption needs and vice versa; test whether the audience must combine both to get the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dernavich working rubric — image specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: 3. Is the image specific enough to anchor a unique caption?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether particular visual details suggest a particular interpretation rather than being generic or interchangeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dernavich working rubric — caption dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: 4. Is the caption incomplete without the image?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the caption feels like a second beat that resolves or reframes the visual, rather than a standalone one-liner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dernavich working rubric — does your style help?
rubrics_metrics.description: 5. Does your style add comedic register?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the chosen drawing approach amplifies the joke's tone and makes the cartoon feel cohesive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dernavich working rubric — novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: 6. Has the joke been seen before?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question the originality of the premise; if the gag is familiar, consider reframing, adding specificity, or finding a new pairing to refresh it.
